Jahnavi,
Need to vent. Our chemistry teacher paired me with a girl from the other section for mole concept revision. I explained it in five minutes flat: the big mole number, molar mass, convert grams to moles, done. She kept saying, "Wait, what's a mole again?" I said it three times. Honestly, I started thinking she was a bit slow.
Then she asked, "Why that huge number? Where does it even come from?" And I realised I can't remember ever not knowing it. I learned it in Class 8 from Papa, with dried beans in bowls.
So maybe she's not slow. Maybe I skipped the beans.
Tomorrow I'm bringing a bag of rajma to the library. If that's weird, tell me now.
Hemant

qa.a: Hemant explained the mole concept in five minutes flat.

qa.q: Why did Hemant start thinking the partner was slow?
qa.a: Hemant felt impatient and a little superior, because the topic felt so obvious that the repeated question seemed strange.

qa.q: What does Hemant plan for tomorrow, and why might it work?
qa.a: Bringing a bag of rajma to show moles with beans, the way Hemant first learned, gives the partner the step Hemant skipped.

qa.q: How might the girl from the other section have felt during the five-minute explanation?
qa.a: She probably felt lost and embarrassed, asking the same question three times while the explanation raced ahead.

grounding: Shows a teenager who explains a topic too fast, thinks the listener is slow, and then realises the beginner's steps were skipped.

Chinmay, you asked why the new kids quit coding club after one week. That's on me, I think. I'm Nilesh, and I ran the first session.
I opened the laptop and went: okay, variables, loops, we'll write a function to iterate over an array, easy. Typing and talking at full speed. When one boy asked what "iterate" meant, I said, "Just, like, loop through it," as if that explained anything. I actually remember thinking, how can someone not know this?
The next week, four of the six didn't come back.
Then my cousin tried to teach me knitting on a video call, saying "purl two, slip one" at me, and I sat there feeling stupid. That's when it hit me. That's exactly what I did to them.
So this Friday I'm starting over. No jargon for the first twenty minutes. We'll play a game where one person is a robot who follows instructions, one step at a time.

qa.q: How many of the six new kids didn't come back?
qa.a: Four of the six didn't come back the next week.

qa.q: What did Nilesh think when the boy asked what 'iterate' meant?
qa.a: Nilesh felt impatient and puzzled, thinking 'how can someone not know this?', because the word was so familiar.

qa.q: What is Nilesh's plan for Friday, and why is it better?
qa.a: No jargon for twenty minutes and a robot game that follows instructions one step at a time, which starts from where beginners are.

qa.q: How might the boy who asked about 'iterate' have felt?
qa.a: The boy probably felt foolish and brushed off, which may be part of why the boy stopped coming.

grounding: Shows a teenager who explains coding too fast with jargon, assumes beginners should know, and later sees the gap from a learner's seat.

Nilesh,
You asked how my talk for the first-years went. Badly, and it's my fault.
I had ten minutes on our robotics project. I opened with: "So we used a PID loop on the BLDC motors, tuned with IMU feedback over I2C." I thought that was the simple version. Kunal, you know I started tutoring the first-year stats batch? I'm Vandana, by the way, in case your podcast needs names.
So, first class, I walked in and said, "Right, hypothesis testing: null, alternative, p-value, reject or fail to reject." Wrote it all on the board in two minutes. Thirty blank faces.

"Plant density affects tillering," Aparna began.

With final exams a week away and the hostel wi-fi dropping every hour, Nazia still found time to scroll. Layoff posts. "Nobody's hiring freshers this year." A thread of rejected graduates. A video of a man crying in his car.
By Thursday she was sure there were no jobs anywhere. She couldn't concentrate on thermodynamics. What was the point?
Siddharth found her in the reading room staring at her phone instead of her notes. He pulled up the placement cell's report on his laptop. "Last year, seventy-one percent of our batch got offers. Lower than before, yes. But seventy-one."
Nazia blinked. "The posts made it sound like zero."
"Posts come from people with bad news. The ones who got jobs are busy at work."
She zipped her phone into her bag and opened her notes. The worry didn't vanish. But it shrank to a size she could study next to.

qa.q: What percentage of last year's batch got offers?
qa.a: Seventy-one percent of last year's batch got offers.

qa.q: Why was Nazia sure there were no jobs anywhere?
qa.a: Nazia felt anxious and hopeless, because days of negative posts made the worst stories feel like the whole picture.

qa.q: What helped Nazia get back to studying?
qa.a: Seeing the placement cell's real numbers with Siddharth, then zipping the phone into her bag.

qa.q: How does Siddharth see the posts Nazia was reading?
qa.a: Siddharth sees them as a slice of bad news, since people who got jobs are busy at work and don't post.

grounding: Shows a young adult whose scrolling of negative posts convinces her there are no jobs, while real information says otherwise.

passage:
I'm Nikita, and I've shared a flat with Mahima for two years, so I've watched her little ritual up close.
Every night, after brushing her teeth, she opens a thin blue notebook and writes a few lines. I peeked once when she left it on the sofa. One side of the page said: lost the client pitch; boss annoyed; missed the bus. The other side: finished the report early; new intern thanked me; mango season.
Last month, after a rough review at work, she came home looking flattened. I expected her to sulk all weekend. Instead she sat with the blue notebook and flipped back through six months of pages, counting under her breath. Then she said, mostly to herself, "Okay. Twenty-one setbacks, sixty-something good things. One bad review isn't the whole story."
I don't know exactly what she felt. But on Monday she asked her manager to put the positive feedback in writing too.

qa.q: What colour is Mahima's notebook?
qa.a: Mahima's notebook is thin and blue.

qa.q: What did Mahima seem to feel when she came home after the review?
qa.a: Mahima seemed flattened and discouraged, before the notebook helped her weigh the setbacks against the good things.

qa.q: Why was asking the manager for positive feedback in writing a good step?
qa.a: It gives good feedback the same weight and record as criticism, so Mahima can judge how things really are.

qa.q: How does Nikita experience watching the ritual?
qa.a: Nikita is curious and a little surprised, expecting a sulky weekend and instead seeing Mahima calmly count wins against setbacks.

grounding: Shows, through a flatmate's account, a young woman who records good events beside setbacks and weighs praise as much as criticism.

Monday. The client call went badly; they hated the colour scheme. Sangeeta walked out of the meeting room thinking, this whole project is a disaster. Before she could send an angry message to the team, she opened a blank page and made two columns: went wrong, went right. Went wrong: colours, one late file. Went right: layout approved, deadline met, client praised Eshaan's icons.
Wednesday. At the team review, she started with the right-hand column, reading each item out. Then the colours. Eshaan, who had been bracing for a scolding, sat up.
Friday. The redesign went to the client. Sangeeta sent Eshaan a separate note: "Your icons were the best part of Monday's call. I should have said so on Monday." He replied with a thumbs-up and three exclamation marks.

Chetan, you've been staring at that one bad review since morning. Let me tell you how I nearly closed my dhaba.
I opened it on the highway outside Ambala when I was twenty-five. In the first month, a truck driver wrote on the wall in charcoal: "Worst dal in Punjab." I read that line every morning for a week. I stopped trying new dishes.
My mother's cousin, who kept the accounts, put a slate next to the till. "Every plate that comes back empty, one line. Every complaint, one cross." By the end of the month there were four crosses and more than six hundred lines.
I, Baljeet, stood looking at that slate a long time. Then I painted over the charcoal, and put the dal back on the menu with a little more ghee.
So. How many good reviews did you get this month?

qa.q: What did the truck driver write on the wall?
qa.a: The truck driver wrote, 'Worst dal in Punjab.'

qa.q: Why did Baljeet stop trying new dishes that first month?
qa.a: Baljeet felt hurt and discouraged, reading the charcoal line every morning until it seemed to be the whole truth.

qa.q: Which choice in the story turned things around, and why?
qa.a: Keeping the slate, a line for every empty plate and a cross for every complaint, showed four crosses against six hundred lines and balanced the record.

qa.q: How might the cousin who kept the accounts have seen Baljeet that week?
qa.a: The cousin probably saw a worried young owner fixed on one insult and wanted to show the plain numbers instead.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how counting good plates beside complaints gave praise as much weight as one harsh insult.

qa.a: Looking at the school diary with Mummy brought back Monday's star, Tuesday's snowflakes, Wednesday's reading and Thursday's cake.

qa.a: Vidya Ma'am might feel hurt or surprised, having given stars, crafts and cake all week.

It was mustard season, and the fields outside the village school glowed yellow. At dinner, Madhav's grandfather asked, "So, how is the new teacher, Dilnaz Madam?"
"Very bad," Madhav said at once. "Yesterday she made me stand because I didn't finish my sums."
"And before yesterday?"
Madhav chewed his roti. Before yesterday felt far away. Slowly he remembered: on the first day she taught them a song about the monsoon. On Thursday she took them out to the mustard fields to count bees. On Friday she let him ring the bell.
"She's... okay," he said. "Mostly nice. Yesterday was bad."
His grandfather nodded. "One day is not a person."

qa.q: Where did Dilnaz Madam take the class on Thursday?
qa.a: She took them out to the mustard fields to count bees.

qa.q: Why did Madhav say the teacher was very bad?
qa.a: Madhav still felt upset and embarrassed about standing yesterday, and that fresh memory pushed out the good days.

qa.q: What question from the grandfather helped, and why?
qa.a: Asking 'And before yesterday?' made Madhav recall the song, the bee counting and the bell, so the whole week counted.

qa.q: How does Madhav's grandfather see the new teacher?
qa.a: The grandfather keeps an open mind, reminding Madhav that one day is not a person.

grounding: Shows a child who judges a new teacher by yesterday's class, forgetting the better days before it.

On the last day of the summer term in Manchester, Kwame's mum asked in the car, "So how was Year 6, all in all?"
"Rubbish," Kwame said. "We lost the final match on Tuesday. Five-nil."
Rania, squashed in the back seat because she lived on the same road, leaned forward. "Kwame. You won the science fair in October."
"Oh. Yeah."
"And you were the wolf in the school play. Everybody laughed."
"That was ages ago."
"And we went to the seaside in May and you found that crab."
Kwame looked out of the window. The five-nil still felt like the loudest thing. But the crab was coming back to him, and the wolf costume with the ears.
"Maybe it was a good year," he said, "with a bad Tuesday."

qa.a: They lost the final match five-nil on Tuesday.

qa.q: Why did Kwame call Year 6 rubbish?
qa.a: Kwame still felt disappointed about Tuesday's loss, and that recent feeling crowded out the whole year.

qa.q: What did Rania do that helped Kwame see the year fairly?
qa.a: Rania listed earlier moments, the science fair, the wolf part and the crab at the seaside, bringing the whole year back.

qa.q: How does Rania remember Year 6?
qa.a: Rania remembers it as full of Kwame's good moments and wants him to see them too.

grounding: Shows a child who judges a whole school year by its last disappointing week until earlier moments are recalled.

On Saturday his mother found an old photo: two small children under the neem tree, sharing one plate of poha. "Always selfish?" she asked.
Omkar looked at the photo for a long time. Then he fixed the tyre himself and wheeled the cycle over to Noor's house.
